title: Water at Madyan
hookLine: Musa waters two women's flock, then sits in the shade and prays: I am in need of whatever good You send

cards: New city, no job, no friends yet, phone at two percent, a bench, and no idea what happens next. That's roughly where Musa is.
He has walked out of Egypt with nothing, down a long desert road, to a well at a place called Madyan. A whole crowd of shepherds is jostling there, watering their animals.
Off to one side, two young women hold their sheep back, waiting. He asks what's wrong. They say: we can't water until the shepherds have gone, and our father is a very old man.
He's exhausted, a stranger, a fugitive.

teach.b: Surah al-Qasas tells it in a few words: so he watered their flock for them. No speech. No asking who they are or what's in it for him.
He does the heavy thing in front of him and pushes through the crowd with their sheep. Then comes the part people remember.

teach.h: I AM IN NEED OF ANY GOOD.
teach.b: He turns away to the shade and prays: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.
The word for in need is faqir, the ordinary Arabic word for poor. A man raised in Pharaoh's palace, sitting in the shade, telling Allah he's poor. He doesn't ask for a job, a wife, or a way home.
Whatever good. And look at the order: he helps first, then asks. The help wasn't a bargain; the prayer isn't a bill.
Then the good arrives, walking. One of the two women comes back, the Qur'an says, walking shyly: my father invites you, to reward you for watering for us.
The old man hears his story and tells him: don't be afraid, you're safe from the wrongdoing people.
One daughter says: father, hire him; the best one to hire is the strong and the trustworthy. By the end of the passage Musa has work, a home and a wife, for eight or ten years of shepherding.
The Qur'an doesn't name the old man. Some commentators identify him with the prophet Shu'ayb; others say he was someone else. Whatever good.
It came in the shape of a family.

how: Musa's words from Surah al-Qasas, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me, are a prayer Muslims use when looking for work, a home, or a way forward.

o: poor, in need of whatever good comes
rich, with more than he needs

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: waited for the shepherds to leave

s: Musa asked the women for payment before helping
he watered their flock and turned away to the shade. the invitation came afterward.
the Qur'an names the old man of Madyan
it doesn't. some commentators identify him with Shu'ayb; others disagree.
Musa's prayer asks for whatever good Allah sends
not a job or a home by name: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down.

games.q: you're Musa. you've just watered the two women's flock at the well. you're alone, tired and a stranger. what do you do next?
o: follow them home to ask for a meal.
sit in the shade and pray: I am in need of any good.
ask the shepherds where to find work.
games.why: he turned to the shade and prayed. then one of the women came walking shyly: my father invites you. the good came to him.

practice: Think of one small, heavy thing you could do for someone, carry the groceries, move the chair, answer the email they're dreading, and picture doing it and walking away without waiting for thanks.

Then sit, as if in shade, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can use Musa's words, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me; if not, just sit empty-handed and notice that that's allowed.

wordCard.voice: Faqir, in need: what Musa called himself in prayer, after he'd watered the flock and asked for nothing specific.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 28:24: "in need," the everyday word for poor — Musa's word for himself.

carryVoice: Your line: in need of any good. Rest doesn't have to be earned first. Until tomorrow.
